mcqs.question: A unit test mocks a database call, asserting only that `save()` was invoked with the right arguments. What can this test NOT tell you?
options: Whether your code calls save() at all
Whether the arguments passed to save() are correctly formed
Whether the real database actually accepts that call and behaves as your code assumes it does
Whether the test itself runs quickly
mcqs.explanation: A mocked call only verifies the interaction your code makes — it says nothing about whether a real database would accept those arguments, enforce constraints you assumed, or behave the way the mock was scripted to. Whether save() is called, with what arguments, and test speed are all things the mock-based test does verify.

mcqs.question: Why do teams run a real, containerized Postgres instance in CI rather than testing against a shared, long-lived test database?
options: A shared database is always faster to set up than a container
A containerized instance is scoped to the test run, avoiding a shared database that other runs or people can leave in a dirty, inconsistent state
Containers are required for any database connection to work in CI
A shared test database cannot run real SQL queries
mcqs.explanation: The core benefit is isolation — a per-run container starts clean and is torn down after, so no test run is affected by leftover state from another run or another person's manual testing. Containers aren't inherently faster to set up, aren't required for CI database connections generally, and a shared database runs real SQL just fine — the problem is state, not query capability.

mcqs.question: What problem does contract testing solve that a full live integration test between two services doesn't have to deal with?
options: It removes the need for either service to have any automated tests
It verifies the same agreement between consumer and provider without requiring both services to be live simultaneously during either one's test run
It only works when both services are written in the same language
It replaces the need for unit tests entirely
mcqs.explanation: Contract testing checks that a consumer's expectations match a provider's real behavior using a shared contract artifact, so neither service needs to be running when the other's tests execute — avoiding the cost and fragility of standing up both live. It doesn't remove the need for tests, isn't language-dependent, and doesn't replace unit testing.

mcqs.question: In consumer-driven contract testing, whose CI pipeline is responsible for replaying a contract against a real implementation?
options: The consumer's CI, replaying its own contract against its own mock
The provider's CI, fetching every consumer's published contract and verifying its real implementation against each one
A third-party service unrelated to either consumer or provider
Neither — contracts are only checked manually during code review
mcqs.explanation: The provider's own CI fetches published consumer contracts and replays them against its real implementation, failing the build if reality no longer matches what a consumer expects — that's what catches a breaking change before it reaches production. The consumer only authors the contract against a mock; it doesn't verify the provider's real behavior itself, and this isn't a manual review step.

mcqs.question: A team's in-memory fake database has quietly drifted from how the real production database actually handles null values. What does this scenario illustrate about lightweight substitutes?
options: In-memory substitutes are always faster and therefore always the better choice
Fidelity to the real dependency isn't guaranteed to stay accurate over time unless someone actively maintains the substitute
This kind of drift is impossible if the fake is well-written initially
Real containerized dependencies have the same drift risk as fakes
mcqs.explanation: A substitute is only as faithful as it was built to be, and that fidelity can erode as the real dependency evolves unless actively kept in sync — exactly what a real containerized dependency avoids by being the actual thing. Speed doesn't make a substitute unconditionally better, drift is a real ongoing risk regardless of initial quality, and real dependencies don't share this particular risk.

mcqs.question: A team's integration test suite passes reliably when run alone but fails intermittently when run in parallel with other tests. What does this pattern most strongly suggest?
options: The test framework doesn't support parallel execution
Tests are sharing mutable database state without proper isolation, causing order- or timing-dependent failures
The database itself has a hardware fault
Parallel test runs always produce some acceptable failure rate
mcqs.explanation: Passing alone but failing under parallel execution is the signature symptom of shared mutable state — tests stepping on each other's data without isolation like transactional rollback. It isn't a framework limitation, isn't evidence of a hardware issue, and intermittent failure under parallelism is a real bug to fix, not an expected baseline.
